source.title: Discovering Cross-Language Reasoning Invariance in LLMs with Geometry-Invariant Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-language feature sharing and functional interchangeability using SAE similarity metrics and causal feature patching, a different measurement recipe from the original claim sources.
record.gate_note: The study measures cross-language sharing within individual language models on paired reasoning traces. It does not test vision-language alignment, independently initialized seeds, or recurrence of identical features across models. Results cited from prior work are not included as rows. Same-language controls are described as near-zero disruption but no separate numerical result is reported for them.
record.test_reason: The study measures how much one model's internal features are shared across languages for the same problem, within each of five LLMs. No version of the claim is about that. V1, V3, V4 and V5 concern alignment between different, independently trained models. V2 is vision–language. V6 and V7 concern the measurement and causes of that cross-model convergence. The paper's link to the hypothesis is an argument: it cites Huh et al. and argues that geometric convergence does not imply functional interchangeability. That argument rests on results for a different construct. Most rows also compare the authors' own contrastive SAE (GI-SAE), which induces sharing on purpose, with a baseline SAE. These are method-performance results, not rates of convergence arising on its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that cross-language feature sharing is model- and depth-dependent: progressive in Qwen, saturated in Gemma, low or mixed in Llama and Phi. GI-SAE raises CKA nearly everywhere, but KL/feature improves mainly in the convergent profile (83% win rate) and not in the saturated one (6%). Geometric similarity should therefore not proxy for functional interchangeability, and sharing must be analysed per model. They add that GI-SAE mainly amplifies sharing already present, and that baseline shared fraction acts as a diagnostic.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multilingual SAE feature sharing, CKA/Jaccard, and causal swapping of shared SAE feature values; it is not the original studies' method of comparing independently trained model representations or seed-level feature subspaces.
record.method_sensitivity: Functional outcomes vary by model, layer, baseline-sharing profile, and patching normalization convention. The authors report stable Qwen results but flips in several low/mixed-profile layers under normalized-space patching.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline within-model cross-language SAE feature sharing on paired MGSM reasoning traces differs strongly by model: Gemma 87–96%, Qwen rising with depth to 51–62%, Phi 1–17%, Llama 4–6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multilingual LLMs share internal features across languages for the same reasoning problem, to a degree that depends on model family and depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastively increasing CKA/Jaccard similarity between languages does not reliably make shared features causally interchangeable. GI-SAE wins on KL/feature in 83% of convergent-profile layers, 49% of low-sharing layers and 6% of saturated layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric representational similarity (CKA) does not imply functional interchangeability under causal patching.

fits_no_version.finding: The most consistently shared features across languages encode answer-boundary, answer-transition and step-format markers. These categories appear in Qwen, Gemma, Llama and Phi, but the paper does not show the same feature recurring across models (Appendix I, Table 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared cross-language features in LLMs concentrate on discourse and answer-boundary structure.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
record.problems: The model sample is small and only Qwen provides a within-family scale comparison. Llama and Phi have about 60 valid problems each. Results use MGSM only and are conditioned on correct solutions with extractable reasoning traces in all six languages. Layer-level confidence intervals are interpreted descriptively because layers within a model are correlated. The normalization sensitivity check covers only representative layers.
record.rows_left_out: The 78 layer-by-layer observations in Appendix B are not each listed separately; model-level and profile-level aggregates plus reported layer-specific win locations are retained. Individual per-layer AFR, shared-fraction, and KL/feature entries in Tables 4–8 are omitted because the selected rows already capture the reported model/profile outcomes. Detailed control values in Table 9 are represented by aggregate pass-rate rows R19–R20.

untested.parts: No comparison of independently trained models' representations against each other. The Qwen 1.7B/4B pair is used only for within-model cross-language sharing.
No mapping, stitching or relative representation between different models. Feature swaps are between languages within one model.
No identification of the same feature across models. The audit reports shared feature categories only.
No cross-model convergence measure is varied. The CKA-vs-causal gap concerns within-model cross-language sharing.
No measure of cross-model alignment levels or of their causes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V1, V4, V6 and V7, but every comparison is within a single model across languages, or between the authors' two SAE variants. None compares representations of different models, which every version requires. The paper's methodological point (CKA can overstate functional equivalence) resembles V6 but applies to a different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. The record's V4 'challenges' label (R4, R9, R18) also misused rows not linked to V4. Workshop paper, small sample (five models, MGSM only).

versions.untested_parts: Only Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B provide a within-family size comparison. The study does not test a broad scale or capability trend across different architectures, objectives, or training data, or establish that increasing performance raises alignment.
No vision-language model pair or image-caption representation alignment is tested.
No comparison across random initializations or seeds of the same architecture is tested.
Tests swapping shared SAE feature values between language traces within one model. It does not test linear maps, stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
The feature audit reports recurring categories of discourse structure, not recurrence of the same feature or circuit across different models.
Tests CKA, Jaccard/shared-feature measures, causal patching, layer dependence, and a limited normalization-convention check. Does not test different neighbour counts or out-of-distribution inputs.
Finds model-specific and incomplete sharing, but does not identify shared training data or objectives as the cause, nor compare those causes against a common model of reality.

conditions.value: English, German, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese

rows.note: The appendix states that baseline sharing increases monotonically from 11% at L16 to 62% at L26.
rows.check: Measures within-model cross-language SAE feature sharing in Qwen3-1.7B, not alignment between independently trained models. The 1.7B vs 4B pair does not make it a cross-model scale test of V1. Values (11–62%) are read correctly.

rows.check: Same construct issue as R1: within-model cross-language sharing, not cross-model convergence. Values 13–51% are correct (Table 5: 13.5–51.4%).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Both show progressive sharing, but the reported layer ranges do not establish that the larger checkpoint is more aligned; this is only a narrow same-family scale comparison (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, same-problem cross-language patches
reader_labels.reason: GI-SAE lowers KL/feature on every tested layer for both Qwen models, indicating improved functional interchangeability in this setting (R6, R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Functional improvement is limited to some layers rather than consistent across the sweep (R8, R10).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: GI-SAE wins on 0/16 layers despite high baseline sharing; the contrastive change does not improve functional interchangeability here (R4, R9, R18).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Across models and layers, geometric versus causal measures
reader_labels.reason: CKA improves in every model-level summary while functional wins vary substantially by model and baseline-sharing profile, showing geometric improvement is not a reliable proxy for interchangeability (R6–R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The Qwen results and aggregate win rate are stable, but several individual low- or mixed-profile layer outcomes change under normalized-space patching (R21).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Baseline sharing across the five tested models
reader_labels.reason: Baseline cross-language sharing ranges from 4–6% in Llama and 1–17% in Phi to 87–96% in Gemma, with distinct model profiles rather than uniform near-complete alignment (R1–R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Models and task conditions in this study
reader_labels.reason: The taxonomy is descriptive, with only one checkpoint for each non-Qwen family, one reasoning dataset, and results conditioned on correct traces in all six languages; the cause of the differing profiles is not established (R1–R5, R16–R18).
